prompt: With no label, what can a clustering be judged by?
hint: Three things, one of them measurable.

choices.text: Stability, a description, and use
choices.why: Yes. The first can be measured, the other two practised.

choices.text: Its accuracy on a test set
choices.why: There is no label to be accurate about.

choices.text: The number of clusters it finds, the more the better for marketing
choices.why: More clusters are not better; four was the stable answer.

choices.text: Its AUC
choices.why: AUC needs a label.

prompt: Finding structure in rows with no label to check against is called ___ learning.
hint: The opposite of every earlier lesson.

prompt: Put the steps of k-means in order.
items: Give each row to its nearest centre
Move each centre to the average of its rows

prompt: Why does `KMeans` take `n_init=10`?
hint: Where it stops depends on where it starts.

choices.text: It uses ten processors
choices.why: Nothing to do with processors.

choices.text: It starts ten times and keeps the lowest inertia
choices.why: Yes. Different starts can stop in different places.

choices.text: It finds ten clusters
choices.why: That is `n_clusters`.

choices.text: It runs ten rounds
choices.why: It runs until nothing moves.

prompt: Cluster 2 in `kmeans.py` is the fruit cluster. What does the number 2 tell you?

choices.text: It is the second most important cluster
choices.why: The numbers carry no rank.

choices.text: It holds the second largest share of customers
choices.why: It is in fact the largest, 345.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Yes. Name clusters by what they hold.

choices.text: Two of its columns are above average
choices.why: The number is just an order of discovery.

prompt: Without scaling, what decided the k-means clusters on `baskets.csv`?
hint: Which column has the largest spread?

choices.text: All columns equally
choices.why: That is what scaling would have done.

choices.text: `orders_month`
choices.why: Its spread of 1.1 made it count for almost nothing.

choices.text: The fruit share
choices.why: It counted, but far less than the basket.

choices.text: `avg_basket`, with a spread of 68.8
choices.why: Yes. The unscaled clusters line up by basket size.

prompt: What adjusted Rand index do two clusterings get when they group the rows identically but number the groups differently?
hint: The labels' names do not matter.

prompt: Which of these methods need the columns scaled first? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A decision tree
choices.why: A split compares a column only with itself.

choices.text: k-means
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Nearest neighbours
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: DBSCAN
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Inertia was 1,778 at k = 4 and 1,659 at k = 5. By how much did it fall?
Why can the lowest inertia not be used to choose k?
hint: What happens to inertia as k grows?

choices.text: It always falls as k rises
choices.why: Yes. One centre per customer would make it zero.

choices.text: It is computed on unscaled columns
choices.why: It was computed on the scaled ones here.

choices.text: It needs a label
choices.why: It needs only distances.

choices.text: It rises after the elbow
choices.why: It keeps falling, only more slowly.

prompt: On real data the silhouette peaks at 2 and the marketing team can handle five newsletters. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: The number also comes from the use.

choices.text: Use 5, because that is what the team can write
choices.why: Capacity is a ceiling, not a reason by itself.

choices.text: Find a stable grouping of five or fewer
choices.why: Yes. Measurements, stability and use together.

choices.text: Use 2, because the silhouette is the measurement
choices.why: Two halves are always fairly clean; that peak says little.

choices.text: Use DBSCAN, since it needs no k
choices.why: It needs eps instead, which is harder to choose.

prompt: DBSCAN gives rows near no core the label ___.
At eps = 1.5 DBSCAN found three clusters, one of them 687 customers. What happened?

choices.text: The noise points formed a cluster of their own
choices.why: There was no noise at 1.5.

choices.text: The data was not scaled
choices.why: Same scaled data at every eps.

choices.text: Two groups came close enough to join
choices.why: Yes. A larger eps connects what a smaller one kept apart.

choices.text: There really are three kinds of customer
choices.why: The range from 1.0 to 1.2, and three other methods, say four.

prompt: What is the honest way to choose eps?

choices.text: Choose the eps with the least noise
choices.why: At 2.0 there is no noise and one cluster.

choices.text: Pick the expected count
choices.why: That finds what you already believed.

choices.text: Use the default
choices.why: The default knows nothing about these units.

choices.text: Look for a range that holds still
choices.why: Yes. Here it held from 1.0 to 1.2.

prompt: Match each linkage to how it measures the distance between two clusters.

pairs.right: The average over all pairs of rows
How much the spread inside clusters would grow

prompt: Single linkage gave one cluster of 687 and one of a single customer. What is this behaviour called?

choices.text: Chaining
choices.why: Yes. A chain of close rows joins two groups.

choices.text: Calibration
choices.why: That is about chances.

choices.text: Overfitting the data
choices.why: There is no label to overfit.

choices.text: Leakage
choices.why: Nothing from a test set is involved.

prompt: Refitted on random halves, k = 4 agreed with the full fit at 1.000 and k = 6 as low as 0.812. What follows?

choices.text: Six is better, since it is more detailed about the customers
choices.why: Detail that changes with the sample is not about the customers.

choices.text: Four describes the customers; six, the sample
choices.why: Yes. The extra groups depend on which half was drawn.

choices.text: The halves were too small to say anything
choices.why: They were 600 customers each, and four came back exactly.

choices.text: Both are equally stable
choices.why: 0.812 is clearly less stable than 1.000.

prompt: How does the lesson suggest finding out whether the bakery cluster is useful?

choices.text: Raise k until the bakery cluster splits
choices.why: Splitting is not testing.

choices.text: Check its silhouette alone
choices.why: A silhouette says it is tight, not that it is useful.

choices.text: Test it on a random half
choices.why: Yes. Test it like any hypothesis.

choices.text: Ask the bakery team whether it looks right
choices.why: An opinion is not a test.

prompt: The smallest cluster holds 184 of 1,200 customers. What percentage is that, to the nearest whole number?
Which of these counted as evidence that the four groups are in the data? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Four came back from every random half
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Ward and average linkage agreed with k-means
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The cluster numbers were 0 to 3
choices.why: Numbers mean nothing.

choices.text: DBSCAN found four over a range of eps
choices.why: Yes.
